newsitem.title: INDIA: Pressure mounts on Indian government over strike.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Indian government over strike.

text.p: Political pressure built on Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda to bow to trade unions' demands on Thursday as a nationwide strike paralysed mail distribution and disrupted phone services for the second day.
The two main communist parties came out in support of the unions' demands for the elimination of a ceiling on annual bonus payments.
The telecommunications minister said he sympathised with the strikers and would present their case to the government.
About one million telecommunications and postal workers launched an indefinite strike on Wednesday over the wage dispute.
The Communist Party of India (CPI), part of Deve Gowda's 13-party minority coalition, issued a statement expressing its solidarity with the striking workers.
The party said a 3,500 rupee ($100) ceiling on annual bonus payments had already been raised for port, dock and railway workers.
Virtually all postal services were shut down, authorities said. Telecommunications services were only partially disrupted as most calls are routed through automatic exchanges.

"The strike is almost 100 percent but due to modern equipment, the public may feel its effects some days later," Suresh Kumar, a trade union leader and former secretary of the Bharatiya (Indian) Telecom Employees Federation, told Reuters.
New Delhi normally pays most junior employees an annual bonus during the Hindu festive season starting in October.
The bonus is usually raised each year but the government this year decided not to increase the payment for postal and telecommunications employees as part of an austerity programme.
Kumar said between 20 and 25 percent of the telecommunications and postal workers received bonuses under the 3,500-rupee ceiling.

The Communist Party of India-Marxist, which backs Deve Gowda's government but is not part of the ruling coalition, said "there is no justification in retaining the ceiling on postal and telecom employees".

Communications Minister Beni Prasad Varma told reporters: "I myself am a pro-labour leader and sympathetic to their demands". He said he would "advocate" the striking workers' case within the government.
But he called the strike illegal, saying trade unions had not give the mandatory 14-day notice to the government.
"We want the minister to act as our spokesman who can put forward our case," Kumar said.
In June last year, authorities called out troops to restore disrupted telephone services in a five-day strike by about 450,000 telecommunications workers.
The strike had been in protest against the government's moves to end a state monopoly on telephones.
